Diagnosis is confirmed if the patient has viral illness symptoms (malaise, fever, pallor) and/or signs (hemolysis, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly), as well as documented babesial parasitemia via polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test or thin slide peripheral smear. C
Treat all symptomatic patients with documented presence of babesial parasitemia because of the risk of complications. C
Atovaquone plus azithromycin (or clindamycin plus quinine) for 7 days to 10 days is recommended as the initial therapy for babesiosis. A
Patients with severe disease or patients refractory to initial therapy should have a partial or complete red blood cell exchange transfusion. C

background.definition: Babesiosis is an emerging, tick-transmitted, zoonotic disease caused by hemotropic parasites of the genus Babesia. The spectrum of disease is broad, ranging from silent infection to a fulminant, malaria-like disease that may result in severe hemolysis and occasionally death.

list.listitem: The incidence of babesiosis is difficult to determine because the initial symptoms may be mild or absent. Although known to be present worldwide, most cases have been reported in the coastal areas of the northeastern and the upper midwestern United States.
The epidemiology of human babesiosis has changed over the past 50 years, with certain parts of the northeastern and midwestern United States now having endemic areas.
Babesia microtti: most common cause of human infection
Babesia duncani: cause of all documented infections on the west coast of the United States
Babesia divergens: primary cause of infections in Europe
Babesia venatorum: European variant
The parasite is transmitted to humans by tick vector (Ixodes scapularis).
The incubation period after transmission can be anywhere from 1 week to 9 weeks.
Avoid areas where ticks, mice, and deer are known to thrive, especially from May through October. C

If traveling or residing in areas where babesiosis is known to be endemic, wear clothing that covers the lower body and tuck pants into socks or stockings. Also, spray clothes with permethrin and apply DEET-containing products to exposed skin. C
After traveling through high-risk areas, a tick check should be performed and attached ticks removed with tweezers as soon as possible. C
Consider the diagnosis of babesiosis in individuals who present with symptoms of viral illness and with recent travel to endemic areas or exposure to persons traveling to these areas. C

Diagnosis is confirmed if the patient has viral illness symptoms (malaise, fever, pallor) and/or signs (hemolysis, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly), as well as documented babesial parasitemia via PCR test or thin slide peripheral smear. C
Common species of babesia include B. microtti (northeast United States), B. duncani (west coast United States) and B. divergens (Europe). C
Patients may be classified as having asymptomatic, mild to moderate, or severe disease. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Erythema chronicum migrans present; no response to antibabesial therapy

list.listitem: Detailed history is prompted by complaints of viral-like illness with reported typical symptoms including, but not limited to: fever, fatigue, and chills.

Evaluation should be considered for any individual reporting the above symptoms after travel to areas of the United States considered endemic for babesial infection (such as Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, and New Jersey).
Physical findings commonly associated with acute babesial infection include fever and pallor. Occasionally, mild splenomegaly and/or hepatomegaly may also be present.

Jaundice, retinal infarcts, ecchymosis, and petechiae may be indicative of a more severe case, especially in immunocompromised patients. Other indicators of severe disease include high-grade parasitemia (≥10%); significant hemolysis; or renal, hepatic, or pulmonary compromise.

Babesiosis may be characterized as: (1) asymptomatic, (2) mild to moderate (commonly associated with B. microtti infection and gradual onset of malaise followed by typical physical findings), or (3) severe (occurs in patients with underlying immunosuppression: HIV, malignancy, immunosuppressive medication, or splenectomy). Babesia divergens infection should be considered a severe disease because of its higher morbidity and mortality rates.

Tests to confirm the diagnosis of babesial infection include hamster inoculation (74% sensitive), Giemsa stain of thin blood smears (84% sensitive), and PCR (95% sensitive). These values come from a single small study of 19 patients with acute babesiosis and 5 patients with similar symptoms but no babesiosis. All patients without babesiosis had negative test results, but as there were only 5 of them, the specificity of 100% has a broad confidence interval around it.

A comparison of real-time PCR assays to conventional PCR on specimens submitted to the CDC found that the test with the highest sensitivity (100%) and specificity (100%) for B. microtti infection was the 18S Taqman.
Multiple blood smears should be done because less than 1% of erythrocytes will show parasitosis in the first week, which is when patients usually seek medical attention.
Microscopic identification of the tetrad form (called the Maltese cross) is pathognomonic of smaller Babesia species such as B. microtti and B. duncani.

Consider babesiosis in patients with flulike symptoms if the person has had recent travel to or lives in an area endemic for babesiosis (usually northeastern United States) or has had a blood transfusion from a similar person. Also consider babesiosis in patients with a recent tick (Ixodes genus) bite. Physical findings include fever, pallor, and splenomegaly with or without hepatomegaly.
Confirm the diagnosis by Giemsa-stained thin blood smears or PCR amplification of Babesial DNA.

Babesiosis may be characterized as: (1) asymptomatic, (2) mild to moderate (commonly associated with B. microtti infection and gradual onset of malaise followed by typical physical findings), or (3) severe (occurs in patients with underlying immunosuppression: HIV, malignancy, immunosuppressive medication, or splenectomy).
Treat all symptomatic patients with documented babesial parasitemia, and consider treatment for asymptomatic patients with documented babesial parasitemia that persists for more than 3 months. C
A combination of atovaquone plus azithromycin or clindamycin plus quinine for 7 days to 10 days is recommended as the initial therapy for babesiosis. A
Patients with severe disease and those refractory to initial therapy should have partial or complete red blood cell exchange transfusion. C
Consider treatment for Lyme disease and/or human granulocytic anaplasmosis in patients with severe disease or persistent symptoms despite appropriate antibabesial therapy. C
Patients with active babesiosis (the presence of flulike symptoms and positive identification of babesial parasites) should be treated with antimicrobial therapy because of the risk of complications.
Treatment is not recommended for individuals who are asymptomatic and/or not demonstrating confirmed babesial parasites.
Consider treatment in asymptomatic patients with confirmed babesial parasites if parasitemia lasts longer than 3 months.
Initial therapy in adults is a combination of atovaquone (750 mg every 12 hours) and azithromycin (500-1000 mg day 1; 250 mg subsequent days) for 7 to 10 days.

Adult patients with mild-to-moderate disease who do not respond to initial therapy and patients who present with severe disease should be treated with clindamycin (300-600 mg IV every 6 hours or 600 mg orally every 8 hours) and quinine (650 mg every 6 to 8 hours orally).
Clindamycin plus quinine has a higher rate of adverse effects and should not be used as first-line therapy unless a contraindication to azithromycin/atovaquone exists.
Because of the higher morbidity and mortality associated with B. divergens, confirmed cases should be treated with clindamycin, quinine, and exchange transfusion.

An in vitro study of combination tafenoquine-atovaquone has shown its efficacy for the treatment of babesiosis (even atovaquone-resistant B. duncani strains) as well as its effectiveness in preventing subsequent infections (ie, secondary prevention). Human trials are needed to confirm these findings.
Partial or complete red blood cell exchange transfusion is indicated for those with severe babesiosis.

Consider the possibility of coinfection with B. burgdorferi (Lyme disease) or A. phagocytophilum (human granulocytic anaplasmosis) in patients who have severe or persistent symptoms despite appropriate antibabesial therapy.

Consider hospitalization and exchange transfusion if the patient demonstrates signs and symptoms consistent with severe disease (high-grade parasitemia ≥10% and/or significant hemolysis); if the patient is immunocompromised; or if the patient has significant pulmonary, renal, or hepatic compromise.

The prognosis is good if the patient has asymptomatic or mild-to-moderate disease and appropriate antibabesial therapy is started in a timely fashion. Clinical improvement is usually seen within 48 hours of initiation of therapy. B

Mortality from babesiosis is low, except in severe cases (including B. divergens). Mortality was shown to be 5% with B. microtti infection. Hospitalized and immunocompromised patients have mortality rates as high as 9% and 21%, respectively. Approximately one third of cases of B. divergens present as severe cases with fulminant progression resulting in death. B
Immunocompromise (HIV, splenectomy/asplenia, or malignancy) may lead to severe or prolonged episodes of babesiosis. C

Routine follow up with repeat identification of babesial parasitemia at 3 months (and possible retreatment) is not recommended unless the patient is immunocompromised or has asymptomatic, documented babesial parasitemia. C

Initial treatment for children is atovaquone (20 mg/kg every 12 hours up to a maximum 750 mg per dose) and azithromycin (10 mg/kg once on day 1 up to a maximum 500 mg per dose, and 5 mg/kg once per day thereafter up to a maximum 250 mg per dose) for 7 to 10 days.

Treatment for severe or refractory cases is clindamycin (7-10 mg/kg IV or orally every 6 to 8 hours up to a maximum 600 mg per dose) and quinine (8 mg/kg orally every 8 hours up to a maximum 650 mg per dose).
